text: Hey! I’m Niko. Your Vision Investigator Officer.
So you want to know how light becomes sight?
Then watching from out here won't help.
We need to go inside somewhere humans can't.
Click on the SCAN button.
There.
Your first destination.
Here it is. The human eye.
It has several parts, and each one has an important job.
Click or ask Niko about each part to explore what it does.
This tough white outer layer is called the sclera. It protects the eye and helps maintain its shape.
This transparent, curved layer at the front is the cornea. It protects the eye and bends incoming light.
This coloured part is the iris. It controls the size of the pupil.
This opening is the pupil. Light enters the eye through it.
We’ve seen the parts we can see from the outside. Now, let’s look inside.
Click on the Inside View button to see how the eye looks from the inside.
Click or ask Niko about each part to explore what it does.
This space between the cornea and the lens contains a clear fluid called aqueous humour.
It helps nourish the front parts of the eye and helps maintain pressure inside the eye.
Behind the pupil is the eye’s natural crystalline lens.
It is transparent, flexible and biconvex, meaning it bulges outward on both sides.
It can change its shape to help focus light from objects at different distances.
Most of the space behind the lens is filled with a clear, jelly-like substance called vitreous humour.
It helps maintain the shape of the eye.
This inner layer at the back is the retina.
It contains light-sensitive cells that detect light.
Behind the retina is the choroid, a layer rich in blood vessels that supplies the eye with oxygen and nutrients.
Now we’ve explored the main structures of the eye.
But there’s something important we haven’t explored yet.
We know that the retina detects light…
…but how does that information reach the brain?
Let’s follow it.
This bundle is the optic nerve.
It carries visual information from the retina to the brain.
The brain receives and processes this information so that we can see.
So the eye and brain are connected through the optic nerve.
We've been looking at the eye. Now let’s follow what happens when you look at an object.
Vision begins when light from an object reaches the eye.
First, the light passes through the cornea, which bends it.
It then travels through the aqueous humour and enters through the pupil.
Change the brightness and observe what happens to the pupil.
In bright light, the pupil becomes smaller.
In dimmer light, the pupil becomes larger.
The iris controls the size of the pupil and therefore regulates how much light enters the eye.
After passing through the pupil, the light reaches the eye’s crystalline lens.
For a nearby object, the lens becomes more curved so that the light can be focused correctly.
For a distant object, the lens becomes less curved.
This continuous adjustment of the lens to focus objects at different distances is called accommodation.
After passing through the lens and vitreous humour, the light reaches the retina.
The lens forms a real, inverted image of the object on the retina.
But what exactly detects this light on the retina?
The retina contains light-sensitive cells called photoreceptors.
Rods are especially sensitive to low levels of light and help us see in dim conditions.
They mainly provide information about brightness rather than colour.
Cones work best in brighter light and allow us to see colours and fine details.
When light reaches these cells, it is converted into electrical signals.
These signals are passed through the retina toward the optic nerve.
The electrical signals leave the eye through the optic nerve.
The optic nerve carries this visual information to the brain.
The brain receives and processes these signals to produce our visual perception.
Although the image formed on the retina is inverted, our visual experience is not simply a photograph of that retinal image. The brain processes the information carried by the signals.
So seeing is a complete process.
Now you’ve followed the journey from the moment light enters the eye to the moment the brain processes the information.
Your eyes are constantly responding to the world around you—even when you’re not thinking about it.
So here’s something to think about…what happens when the eye cannot focus light properly?
Why might some things look blurry, even when your eyes are working?
